title: The 10 Best Wire Strippers
subtitle: Manual and self-adjusting wire strippers for house wiring, car wiring and electronics, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: A wire stripper removes insulation without nicking the copper, which a knife can't do reliably. We ranked 10 best-sellers from Klein, KNIPEX, IRWIN and value brands on rating, review volume and features (self-adjusting jaws, a crimper, screw or bolt cutters and separate solid and stranded markings). Klein makes three of the ten picks.

changelog.note: Page published with 10 ranked picks and 1 tool to avoid.

avoid.name: Wire Stripper, 3-rd Generation Wire Strippers or Crimping Tool, 5-IN-1 Wire Crimper or Cutter, 10-20 AWG Electric Wire
avoid.flag: Wire range listed two ways; brand spelled two ways
avoid.verdict: A $4 stripper whose listing disagrees with itself on the wire sizes it handles and doesn't even spell its own brand consistently.
reasons: The title says '10-20 AWG' but the bullets say 'a range of 10-22 AWG', so you can't tell whether it strips 22-gauge wire.
The brand field says 'Htaexpu' while the first bullet says 'The Htaxepu Advantage', and the model number is just 'Wire Stripper'.
The bullets explain what wire strippers do in general instead of describing this tool. The WGGE WG-015 is a few dollars more, clearly specified, and has 17,090 reviews.

buyers_guide.a: Manual strippers have a hole for each wire gauge; you pick the hole, squeeze and pull. Self-adjusting (automatic) strippers grip and strip in one squeeze on any size in their range. Automatic is faster for repetitive work; manual is slimmer and more precise in tight boxes.

buyers_guide.q: What's the difference between solid and stranded?
buyers_guide.a: House wiring is usually solid copper; extension cords, car wiring and speaker wire are stranded. Stranded wire of the same gauge is slightly thicker, so better strippers mark separate holes for each.
Most US outlets and lights use 14 AWG (15 A circuits) or 12 AWG (20 A circuits). Strippers rated 10-20 or 10-22 AWG cover both.
If you work on cars, trailers or anything with spade and ring terminals, yes. For outlets and switches, no.
Holes for 6-32 and 8-32 screws let you cut outlet and switch screws to length without ruining the threads.
